concepts.name: Liquidity risk and its causes
concepts.definition: The danger that a bank can't meet short-term obligations or fund asset growth because it can't get cash quickly enough. It's inherent in asset transformation (liquid liabilities fund illiquid assets) and comes from both sides: deposit withdrawals, and loan commitment drawdowns or falling investment values.
misconceptions: Thinking a bank meets liquidity needs by calling in long-term loans

questions.prompt: What is bank liquidity risk?
options: The danger that a bank can't meet short-term obligations or fund asset growth because it can't get cash quickly enough
The risk that interest rates change
The risk that the bank's shares become illiquid
questions.explanation: In the extreme, it becomes insolvency risk through fire sales.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the usual ways a bank meets a liquidity demand?
questions.explanation: Loans are illiquid and hard to call in.

questions.prompt: Why is liquidity risk built into a bank's asset transformation function?
options: Short-term, liquid liabilities (deposits) fund long-term, illiquid assets (loans)
Loans can be withdrawn on demand
questions.explanation: The bank promises repayment on demand while holding assets it can't sell on demand.

questions.prompt: Which is an ASSET-side source of liquidity risk?
options: Borrowers drawing down loan commitments (e.g. Covid-19 'dash for cash')
questions.explanation: The asset side also includes an unexpected fall in the investment portfolio's value (e.g. SVB).

questions.prompt: The value of a bank's investment portfolio falls unexpectedly (as at SVB). What happens to its liquidity risk?
questions.explanation: Assets it might sell for cash are now worth less, so it has less liquidity to call on.
feedback: Lower asset values reduce available cash.
The lecture lists this as an asset-side cause.

questions.prompt: Which three factors does the lecture say matter when measuring liquidity risk?
options: Potential cash flows, the bank's capacity to borrow, and its stock of high-quality liquid assets
Loan rates, deposit rates and fees
questions.explanation: Not all deposits or commitments will be called at once, so the bank assesses likely demands.

questions.prompt: A bank must sell illiquid assets at fire-sale prices to meet withdrawals. What can happen next?
options: Fire-sale losses erode capital, turning a liquidity problem into an insolvency problem
Nothing: selling assets always solves liquidity problems
Depositors are paid less than they're owed by law
questions.explanation: Withdrawals → fire sales → realised losses → capital erodes → possible failure (SVB, Credit Suisse).
feedback: Selling below fair value causes losses.

questions.prompt: In March 2020 many companies drew down their credit lines at once (the 'dash for cash'). Why is this a liquidity problem for banks even though their loans rise?
options: Each drawdown needs cash immediately, so banks must run down cash, sell liquid assets or borrow just as markets are stressed
It isn't: higher loans always improve liquidity
Because deposits automatically fall by the same amount
Because the loans are repaid immediately
questions.explanation: Commitments drawn → cash needed now → banks drain liquid assets or borrow under stress. This is asset-side liquidity risk.
feedback: Loans are illiquid; funding them uses cash.
Drawn funds may be redeposited, but not reliably.

questions.prompt: At SVB, deposits were withdrawn just as rising rates cut the value of its bond portfolio. Which sources of liquidity risk were at work?
options: Both sides: liability-side withdrawals and an asset-side fall in the investment portfolio's value
Neither: it was purely credit risk
questions.explanation: The lecture lists SVB's falling investment values as an asset-side cause; the deposit run was the liability side.
feedback: The fall in bond values was the asset side.
The problem wasn't commitments being drawn.

concepts.name: Net deposit drain: purchased vs stored liquidity
concepts.definition: Net deposit drain = withdrawals − new deposits. Purchased liquidity (borrowing in interbank/repo markets, wholesale CDs) keeps the asset side intact but is costly and dries up when lenders doubt solvency. Stored liquidity (running down cash, selling assets) needs no market but shrinks the balance sheet and means holding low-return assets.
misconceptions: Thinking purchased liquidity is always available

questions.prompt: What is the net deposit drain?
questions.explanation: Managers can usually predict its probability distribution quite accurately.
feedback: That's related to the financing gap.

questions.prompt: What's the main benefit of purchased liquidity management?
options: It insulates the size and composition of the asset side from normal deposit drains
It's the cheapest source of funds
It's always available in a crisis
questions.explanation: The bank borrows to replace the deposits, so its assets stay as they were.
feedback: Market rates are usually higher than deposit rates.
It dries up in a crisis.

questions.prompt: What's the main cost of stored liquidity management?
options: The balance sheet shrinks and the bank must hold low-return assets, forgoing income from loans
questions.explanation: Its benefit is not relying on the market.

questions.prompt: A bank meets a $5m deposit drain by running down cash (stored liquidity). What happens to its total assets?
questions.explanation: Cash and deposits both fall by $5m, so the balance sheet shrinks.

questions.prompt: A bank meets a $5m deposit drain by borrowing $5m (purchased liquidity). What happens to its total assets?
questions.explanation: Borrowed funds replace the lost deposits, so the asset side is untouched.
feedback: Borrowing replaces funding; assets aren't added.

questions.prompt: Withdrawals today are $12m and new deposits $7m. What's the net deposit drain?
questions.explanation: Net drain = withdrawals − new deposits = 12 − 7.

questions.prompt: Why is purchased liquidity least available exactly when a bank needs it most?
options: When lenders doubt the bank's solvency, or in a crisis, they charge more, cut limits or refuse to roll over funds
Regulators ban borrowing in a crisis
Interbank rates fall in a crisis
questions.explanation: Most purchased funding is short-term and must be rolled over repeatedly.
feedback: They can, if lenders will buy them.

questions.prompt: Why do banks typically combine purchased and stored liquidity?
options: Each has a cost: purchased is expensive and unreliable in stress; stored ties up money in low-return assets
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends balancing the trade-off.

questions.prompt: A bank has $10m cash and $8m equity; its loans can only be sold at 80% of book value. A net deposit drain of $30m hits. How much equity is left?
questions.explanation: Cash covers $10m; the other $20m needs $25m of loans sold at 80%, a $5m loss. Equity: 8 − 5 = $3m.
feedback: That takes the loss as 20% of the $10m from loans; it's $20m needed.
That's the loss, not the equity left.

questions.prompt: Same bank ($10m cash, $8m equity, loans sell at 80%). What's the largest drain it can meet before its equity is wiped out?
questions.explanation: Each $1 raised from loans costs $0.25 of loss. Equity covers 8 ÷ 0.25 = $32m from loans, plus $10m cash = $42m.
feedback: That treats the loss as 20% of the cash raised instead of 25%.

concepts.name: Net liquidity statement and peer ratios
concepts.definition: A daily statement of sources (cash-type assets, maximum borrowing available, excess reserves) against uses (borrowed funds already used, assets already repo'd). Peer group ratios: loans-to-deposits, borrowed funds to total assets, commitments to total assets.
misconceptions: Counting required reserves as a source

questions.prompt: Which is a SOURCE of liquidity in the net liquidity statement?
options: Excess cash reserves above required reserves
questions.explanation: Sources: cash-type assets, maximum borrowing available, excess reserves.

questions.prompt: A bank uses more of its available borrowing capacity. What happens to its net liquidity?
questions.explanation: Borrowed funds already used are a use of liquidity.
feedback: More use means less net liquidity.

questions.prompt: A bank's commitments-to-lend relative to total assets rises. What happens to its asset-side liquidity exposure?
questions.explanation: More commitments means more potential drawdowns it must fund.
feedback: It's one of the peer ratios for that reason.

questions.prompt: Cash-type assets $15m, maximum borrowing $40m, excess reserves $3m; already borrowed $25m and $8m of assets repo'd. What's the net liquidity?
A bank's loans-to-deposits and borrowed-funds-to-assets ratios are far above its peers'. What does this suggest?
options: It relies heavily on the short-term money market rather than core deposits to fund loans
It has very low credit risk
questions.explanation: Compare with banks of similar size and location.

questions.prompt: A bank's net liquidity statement shows sources of $75m and uses of $40m. It expects a net deposit drain of $40m tomorrow. What does the statement flag?
options: A $5m shortfall: net liquidity of $35m won't cover the drain, so the bank needs more sources
questions.explanation: Net liquidity = 75 − 40 = $35m, which is $5m short of the expected $40m drain.
feedback: Sources minus uses must still cover the drain.

concepts.name: Liquidity index
concepts.definition: I = Σ wᵢ (Pᵢ ÷ Pᵢ*), where Pᵢ is the fire-sale price and Pᵢ* the fair price if the bank can wait. 0 < I ≤ 1: the higher I, the more liquid the bank's assets.
misconceptions: Reading a lower index as more liquid

questions.prompt: What does the liquidity index measure?
options: The potential loss from selling assets immediately (a fire sale) instead of at fair market value
Cash as a share of deposits
The probability of a bank run
questions.explanation: It compares fire-sale prices with fair prices.

questions.prompt: In this formula, what is Pᵢ*?
options: The fair market price the bank would get if it could wait
questions.explanation: Pᵢ is the immediate sale price; Pᵢ* the price under normal sale conditions.

questions.prompt: Fire-sale prices fall while fair prices are unchanged. What happens to the liquidity index?
questions.explanation: A lower Pᵢ ÷ Pᵢ* means a lower index: less liquid assets.
feedback: Lower fire-sale prices can't raise the index.
The index depends on fire-sale prices.

questions.prompt: Bank A's liquidity index is 0.95 and Bank B's is 0.80. Which is more liquid?
options: Bank A: a higher index means a smaller fire-sale discount
questions.explanation: The higher I, the more liquid the asset portfolio.
feedback: Lower I means bigger fire-sale losses.
The index allows a direct comparison.

questions.prompt: Lecture example: 50% one-month T-bills ($99 today vs $100 at maturity) and 50% real estate loans ($85 today vs $92 at month end). What's the liquidity index?
feedback: That uses face value ($100) as the fair price of the loans.

questions.prompt: Same bank, but a thin real estate market means the loans fetch only $65 today (vs $92 at month end). What's the index?
feedback: That uses $100 as the loans' fair price.

questions.prompt: A bank holds 60% T-bills (fire-sale $98, fair $100) and 40% loans (fire-sale $80, fair $90). What's its liquidity index?
feedback: That uses $100 as the loans' fair price.

concepts.name: Financing gap and financing requirement
concepts.definition: Financing gap = average loans − average (core) deposits. Financing gap + liquid assets = financing requirement = borrowed funds. A widening gap warns of liquidity trouble; lenders may raise premiums, cut limits or refuse to roll over.
misconceptions: Forgetting to add liquid assets to get the financing requirement

questions.prompt: Why are average deposits subtracted in the financing gap?
options: Most demand deposits stay for two years or more, so they're a core source of funding
Deposits are a use of funds
Deposits are always withdrawn within a day
questions.explanation: The gap is the part of the loan book core deposits don't cover.

questions.prompt: Average deposits fall while average loans are unchanged. What happens to the financing gap?
questions.explanation: Less core funding leaves a bigger gap to fund by borrowing or running down liquid assets.

questions.prompt: Average loans are $40m, average deposits $32m and liquid assets $6m. What's the financing requirement?
questions.explanation: Gap = 40 − 32 = 8; requirement = gap + liquid assets = 8 + 6 = $14m.

questions.prompt: Rearrange this to find the financing gap.
options: Financing gap = Borrowed funds − Liquid assets
Financing gap = Borrowed funds + Liquid assets
Financing gap = Liquid assets − Borrowed funds
Financing gap = Borrowed funds ÷ Liquid assets
questions.explanation: The lecture also writes it as: financing gap = −liquid assets + borrowed funds.
feedback: That's the negative of the gap.

questions.prompt: What can a widening financing gap warn of?
options: Future liquidity problems: rising deposit withdrawals and more loan commitments being drawn
questions.explanation: If liquid assets aren't run down, the bank must borrow more.

questions.prompt: A bank's financing requirement keeps rising. How do money-market lenders react, and with what result?
options: They worry about its creditworthiness and charge higher premiums, set stricter limits or refuse to roll over; if the requirement exceeds those limits the bank may become insolvent
They lend more at lower rates
The central bank must take over
questions.explanation: Requirement ↑ → borrowing ↑ → lenders' doubts → costlier, scarcer funding → possible insolvency.
feedback: Lenders get more cautious, not less.

questions.prompt: What is the financing gap?
questions.explanation: It's the part of the loan book core deposits don't cover.

questions.prompt: A bank's financing gap widens from $5m to $9m while it keeps $5m of liquid assets. How much more must it borrow in the money market?
options: Nothing more, because liquid assets are unchanged
questions.explanation: Financing requirement = gap + liquid assets: 5 + 5 = 10 before, 9 + 5 = 14 after.
feedback: That's the new gap, not the change in borrowing.
That's the new total, not the increase.
The gap itself must be funded.

concepts.name: Liquidity planning and bank runs
concepts.definition: Plan by identifying which depositors may withdraw and the likely size of withdrawals over weeks, months and years. A bank run is a sudden, unexpected increase in withdrawals, caused by solvency concerns, a related failure or a shift to non-bank investments. First-come, first-served payment spreads runs; panics are contagious.
misconceptions: Thinking only insolvent banks can suffer runs

questions.prompt: What is a bank run?
options: A sudden, unexpected increase in deposit withdrawals
questions.explanation: Runs are costly and can push even a solvent bank into insolvency.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a cause of bank runs listed in the lecture?
options: A rise in the bank's capital ratio
The failure of a related financial institution
A sudden shift in investor preference towards non-bank investments
questions.explanation: A stronger capital ratio would reassure depositors.

questions.prompt: Why does a bank identify which types of depositors are likely to withdraw?
options: The composition of its depositor base affects how severe a funding shortfall will be
questions.explanation: Planning also estimates deposits and withdrawals over weeks, months and years.

questions.prompt: Deposits are paid first come, first served. When doubts about a bank's solvency arise, what happens to depositors' incentive to withdraw early?
questions.explanation: Your place in line decides whether you're paid in full if the bank fails, so everyone has a reason to go early.

questions.prompt: What is a bank panic?
options: A systemic or contagious run across banks, justified or not
questions.explanation: Examples: Northern Rock, IndyMac and WaMu in the GFC; later Greece and Cyprus.

questions.prompt: A related financial institution fails. How could this push a solvent bank into insolvency?
options: Contagion triggers a run, the bank fire-sells illiquid assets to pay depositors, and the losses wipe out its capital
The bank's loans become more valuable
Depositors move money into the bank
It can't: only insolvent banks fail
questions.explanation: Related failure → run → fire sales → losses → insolvency, even if the bank was solvent beforehand.
feedback: Runs can force solvent banks into insolvency.

questions.prompt: A depositor believes her bank is solvent but sees others queuing to withdraw. Why might withdrawing still be rational?
options: Deposits are paid first come, first served: if others' withdrawals force fire sales and failure, those late in line may not be paid in full
Because interest stops on deposits during a run
It isn't rational: solvency means she is safe
questions.explanation: That self-fulfilling logic is why runs can push even solvent banks into insolvency.
feedback: Not always: but runs can make them fail.
Fire sales can turn a solvent bank insolvent.

concepts.name: Basel III liquidity standards (LCR and NSFR)
concepts.definition: LCR = stock of HQLA ÷ total net cash outflows over the next 30 days ≥ 100%. NSFR = available stable funding ÷ required stable funding > 100% over one year. HQLA: low risk, easy to value, low correlation with risky assets, listed on a developed exchange, active low-volatility market.
misconceptions: Using gross outflows instead of net outflows in the LCR

questions.prompt: What horizon does the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) cover?
questions.explanation: It requires enough HQLA to cover net cash outflows over 30 days of acute stress.

questions.prompt: What does the NSFR aim to ensure?
options: That long-term assets are funded by a minimum of stable liabilities over a one-year horizon
questions.explanation: It matches uses and sources of funds.

questions.prompt: What goes in the LCR's numerator?
options: The stock of high-quality liquid assets
questions.explanation: The denominator is net cash outflows over 30 days.
questions.equation: LCR = \frac{\text{Stock of high quality liquid assets}}{\text{Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days}} \geq 100\%

questions.prompt: Expected 30-day cash inflows rise, with HQLA and gross outflows unchanged. What happens to the LCR?
questions.explanation: Higher inflows reduce net outflows (the denominator), so the LCR rises.
questions.equation: LCR = \frac{\text{Stock of high quality liquid assets}}{\text{Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days}} \geq 100\%

questions.prompt: What did the RBA offer Australian banks to help them meet the LCR?
questions.explanation: Australia had relatively few government securities to use as HQLA.

questions.prompt: A bank has $120m of HQLA, 30-day stressed outflows of $150m and inflows of $60m. What's its LCR?
questions.explanation: Net outflows = 150 − 60 = 90; LCR = 120 ÷ 90 = 133%, above 100%, so it complies.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT counted as available stable funding?
options: Preferred stock with a maturity over one year
Liabilities with maturities over one year
questions.explanation: Stable funding is long-term; overnight borrowing can vanish.

questions.prompt: Which asset best fits the lecture's definition of high-quality liquid assets?
options: Government bonds traded in an active, low-volatility market
Shares in a thinly traded start-up
questions.explanation: HQLA: low risk, easy to value, low correlation with risky assets, listed on a developed exchange, active market.

questions.prompt: A bank has $80m of HQLA, 30-day stressed outflows of $140m and inflows of $50m. Does it meet the LCR, and how much more HQLA would it need?
options: No: LCR is 88.9%; it needs $10m more HQLA
No: LCR is 57.1%; it needs $60m more HQLA
No: LCR is 88.9%; it needs $90m more HQLA
questions.explanation: Net outflows = 140 − 50 = 90; LCR = 80 ÷ 90 = 88.9%. To reach 100% it needs $90m of HQLA: $10m more.
feedback: It needs $90m in total, i.e. $10m more.

questions.prompt: HQLA rises 10% and net cash outflows also rise 10%. What happens to the LCR?
questions.explanation: Both numerator and denominator scale by 1.1, so the ratio is unchanged.
questions.equation: LCR = \frac{\text{Stock of high quality liquid assets}}{\text{Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days}} \geq 100\%
